If the figure above shows the graph of $g(x),$ then

${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{g(x)}{{x}^{2}}=$
 {{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
Applying the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{g(x)}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(g(x)\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }g(x)\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }g(x)=-2.$ Therefore, the above becomes:

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{g(x)}{{x}^{2}}=-2\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}
$$

Now, using the fact that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})=0,
$$

we can evaluate our limit as follows:

$$
-2\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}=-2\cdot 0=0
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{g(x)}{{x}^{2}}=0.
$$
